title: Cloudflare Measures Origin TLS Preferences, Cutting Handshake Retries from 52% to 3.7%
gist: Cloudflare's new Automatic Key Exchange feature replaces a one-size-fits-all X25519 guess with per-origin TLS key-agreement probing, cutting HelloRetryRequests on scanned origins from about 52% to 3.7% and removing over 150ms of p90 handshake latency, while also revealing that post-quantum origin adoption has only reached 12.8% ahead of Cloudflare's 2029 "Q-Day" target.

themes.theme: From static guess to measured per-origin key exchange

insights.claim: Cloudflare replaced a static assumption in its origin TLS handshakes with a per-origin measurement called Automatic Key Exchange, cutting HelloRetryRequests on scanned origins from roughly 52% to 3.7% and removing more than 150 ms from p90 handshake latency.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A roughly 14x reduction in retry rate and >150ms p90 latency cut is a material performance win applicable to any high-traffic CDN or reverse-proxy operator running TLS 1.3 to diverse origins.
insights.locator: Cloudflare has replaced a static assumption in its origin TLS handshakes

insights.claim: TLS 1.3 requires a client to commit to a key agreement algorithm in its first packet before the server has said what it supports; guessing correctly completes the handshake in one round trip, while guessing wrong forces a HelloRetryRequest and a second ClientHello, doubling the connection cost.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Explains the core mechanism driving the whole optimization: any protocol requiring a first-move commitment under uncertainty creates a guessing-cost problem that measurement can solve.
insights.locator: TLS 1.3 requires a client to commit to a key agreement algorithm

insights.claim: Cloudflare had guessed X25519 for every origin on the internet on the reasonable grounds that over 95% of origins support it, but measurement showed that guess was suboptimal for roughly 30% of origin connections, with more than 6% of origins preferring P-256 or P-384 over X25519 and paying an unnecessary extra round trip.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Shows that a seemingly reasonable population-level default (>95% support) can still be wrong for a meaningfully large minority of connections, justifying the shift to per-origin measurement over static heuristics.
insights.locator: Cloudflare guessed X25519 for every origin on the internet

insights.claim: Automatic Key Exchange probes each origin outside the production traffic path, one key agreement group at a time, with origins rescanned daily so preferences track changes to load balancers and TLS libraries; it is on for all existing zones and on by default for new ones, with a dashboard toggle under SSL/TLS, and Cloudflare applies one preference per zone.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Daily rescanning and out-of-band probing means the optimization self-corrects as origin infrastructure changes, reducing operational burden on customers.
insights.locator: Automatic Key Exchange, an extension of Automatic SSL/TLS, probes each origin

insights.claim: Active probing uncovered thousands of origins whose post-quantum support never appeared in passive traffic monitoring, because many origins accept a classical keyshare without issuing a retry even when they support something stronger.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A key methodological finding: passive traffic observation systematically undercounts real origin capability, so any capacity-planning or capability-inventory exercise relying on passive monitoring alone will understate readiness.
insights.locator: Measurement turned out to reveal more than observation had

themes.theme: Post-quantum adoption curve and technical constraints

insights.claim: An X25519MLKEM768 post-quantum keyshare is 1,216 bytes against X25519's 32 bytes, which pushes the ClientHello past a single network packet; although the TLS standard permits multi-packet segments, some legacy middleboxes and origin servers fail when a ClientHello is split across TCP segments, and in Cloudflare's earlier study around 0.34% of scanned origins failed to complete the handshake when sent a post-quantum keyshare first.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A ~38x larger keyshare is not just a bandwidth cost but a compatibility risk with legacy middleboxes, explaining why Cloudflare couldn't simply lead with post-quantum by default.
insights.locator: An X25519MLKEM768 keyshare is 1,216 bytes against X25519's 32

insights.claim: Since September 2023 Cloudflare used HelloRetryRequest as a safety valve, advertising post-quantum support but leading with classical X25519 and requiring capable origins to request the upgrade via retry, which meant almost every post-quantum origin handshake paid a mandatory second round trip.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Explains why the old safety-first design imposed a de facto tax on the very post-quantum-capable origins it was meant to support, a tradeoff the new measurement approach directly resolves.
insights.locator: That is why Cloudflare had been using HelloRetryRequest as a safety valve

insights.claim: Origin support for post-quantum key exchange has grown from 0.5% in 2023 to 12.8% today, meaning roughly seven in eight origins still cannot use it; among the cohort Cloudflare has scanned so far, 64% stayed on classical X25519 unchanged, 33% moved to X25519MLKEM768, and 3% moved to a different classical curve such as P-384, P-256, or P-521.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A ~25x growth in post-quantum origin adoption over three years is fast in relative terms but still leaves the large majority of internet origins unprotected against future quantum decryption, framing the scale of remaining migration work.
insights.locator: The adoption figures give the change its context

insights.claim: For origins that can use post-quantum key exchange, the share of post-quantum origin TLS 1.3 traffic completing without a HelloRetryRequest rose from 0% to 99.2%, and post-quantum origin traffic across the scanned cohort grew from roughly 25 billion to 45 billion connections a day, which Cloudflare attributes in part to Automatic Key Exchange upgrading classical connections.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Nearly doubling post-quantum connection volume (25B to 45B/day) suggests the measurement-driven default change itself is accelerating post-quantum uptake, not just optimizing existing traffic.
insights.locator: For the origins that can use post-quantum key exchange

themes.theme: Operational risk, safe rollout design, and roadmap

insights.claim: A new Compliance requirements setting lets customers restrict Cloudflare to post-quantum-hybrid-only or FIPS-compliant-only key agreements; because these narrow rather than expand what Cloudflare can negotiate, enforcing post-quantum hybrid against an origin that does not support X25519MLKEM768 leaves no mutually supported algorithm and causes all TLS 1.3 connections to that origin to fail, and selecting both options at once is rejected if no algorithm satisfies both.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A concrete misconfiguration trap: teams enabling strict compliance settings without first confirming origin post-quantum support risk taking their own origin offline for TLS 1.3 traffic.
insights.locator: A new Compliance requirements setting carries a risk worth flagging

insights.claim: The Origin Post-Quantum Encryption API remains available but requests to it are now no-ops that do not change a zone's post-quantum key agreement behavior, and Cloudflare plans to deprecate the API without giving a date.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Teams with automation built against that API are silently operating on a no-op today and should migrate before an unannounced deprecation removes it entirely.
insights.locator: Teams with existing automation should note a quieter change

insights.claim: The rollout mechanism is conservative: a new key-exchange preference is applied to a small share of an origin's traffic first while the system monitors failure and retry rates against that origin's baseline, rolling back if retries climb, the same pattern used by Automatic SSL/TLS when an encryption mode upgrade misbehaves, so the worst case of a rollback is an additional round trip rather than a broken connection.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A reusable canary-and-rollback design pattern for any infrastructure change touching live traffic: bound the blast radius, monitor against a baseline, and ensure the failure mode is degraded performance rather than outage.

insights.claim: The latency improvement applies only to new connections, not requests on existing keep-alive connections, and the gain concentrates on dynamic requests and CDN cache misses that require a fresh origin handshake; Automatic Key Exchange also cannot prefer post-quantum key exchange where an origin doesn't support it, though it still helps by learning which classical algorithm an origin prefers.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Sets realistic expectations for who benefits: sites dominated by cache hits and persistent connections will see less improvement than those with frequent fresh origin handshakes.
insights.locator: Two limits are worth noting for teams assessing the benefit

insights.claim: Key agreement encryption alone does not prevent an attacker with a quantum computer from forging a classical certificate to impersonate an origin; Cloudflare has supported ML-DSA post-quantum signatures since mid-2026 in Authenticated Origin Pulls and Custom Origin Trust Store to enable end-to-end post-quantum authentication, but presenting an ML-DSA certificate achieves nothing unless the verifying side also rejects classical certificates.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A critical nuance for security teams: post-quantum key exchange alone is an incomplete defense, and organizations must also enforce rejection of classical certificates to close the impersonation gap.
insights.locator: Key agreement is only half the problem

insights.claim: Cloudflare's roadmap includes moving from per-zone to per-origin preference granularity (since one lagging origin can currently hold back a whole zone), adding on-demand scans via dashboard and API instead of waiting for the next daily scan, and extending scanning to auto-detect ML-DSA support and disable classical fallback for customers wanting strict protection.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Signals Cloudflare intends to keep tightening post-quantum enforcement over time, which customers with mixed-capability origin fleets should plan for.
insights.locator: Three items sit on the roadmap

insights.claim: Cloudflare frames the work against a 2029 target it calls Q-Day, the year some industry estimates suggest classical encryption could be breached, and against harvest-now decrypt-later attacks where recorded traffic is stored for future decryption once quantum computers are capable.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete deadline framing for why post-quantum migration urgency is rising now rather than being deferred indefinitely, useful context for infrastructure and security budget planning.
insights.locator: Cloudflare frames the work against a 2029 target it calls Q-Day
